content: 1. Some data for assessing access to hygienic sanitation facilities is collected through Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS), Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys (MICS), and national surveys. However, there are methodological challenges associated with this data collection process. 2. The Integrated Global Action Plan for the Prevention and Control of Pneumonia and Diarrhoea (GAPPD) defines indicators and sources of data to evaluate progress. For example, access to improved drinking water is measured by the percentage of households and healthcare facilities reporting the use of an improved water source, with data sourced from DHS, MICS, and national surveys. 3. The use of household water treatment and safe storage is assessed by the percentage of households and healthcare facilities with an observed treatment method or product, supplemented by water quality testing in a subset of households. This data is also collected through DHS, MICS, and national surveys. 4. Household air pollution is evaluated by the percentage of households using clean fuels for cooking. Data for this indicator is sourced from the WHO Household Energy Database, which includes DHS, MICS, Living Standards Measurement Study, national surveys, and censuses. 5. WHO, in collaboration with the World Bank and other SEFA (Sustainable Energy for All) partners, is developing a multi-tiered framework to set targets and monitor progress in access to modern energy for households and community services, pollutant emission levels, and electricity supply. This framework will be tested and refined for implementation within two to three years. 6. Achieving global objectives for pneumonia and diarrhoea control requires coordination of relevant programs at country and regional levels, as well as expanded support from development agencies and emergency response organizations. Partners are encouraged to align their support with government-led action plans and priorities. 7. The GAPPD goals align with the Global Strategy for Women’s and Children’s Health and the Every Woman Every Child (EWEC) movement, particularly the call to action from Committing to Child Survival: A Promise Renewed. A core group of international partners, including UN agencies and technical institutions, has led the development of GAPP and GAPPD, with specific activities assigned based on expertise and interest. 8. Within the UN system, WHO and UNICEF have a leading role in child survival efforts due to their combined expertise and experience. Many international governmental and non-governmental organizations are already providing or planning to provide assistance to developing countries to build and sustain national capacity for pneumonia and diarrhoea control in young children. 9. These activities are often integrated into broader efforts to address Millennium Development Goal (MDG) 4, which targets a reduction in child mortality. Supportive activities must be maintained and enhanced, with specific emphasis on pneumonia and diarrhoea, and sustained beyond 2015. 10. Regional and international agencies are expected to provide technical assistance for country-level activities and facilitate opportunities for country-to-country exchange of experiences. These activities may include revising, adapting, and developing technical, operational, and managerial policies; pricing vaccines, drugs, and equipment; and presenting concise technical programs with cost and outcome projections. 11. UNICEF and its partners are working closely with manufacturers to increase the availability of zinc, as UNICEF is the largest buyer of zinc tablets, accounting for over 80% of international procurement. UNICEF is also the largest procurer of dispersible amoxicillin tablets. 12. Key partners can contribute significantly to addressing risk factors beyond the health sector, such as improving access to clean household energy. National groups coordinating pneumonia and diarrhoea control can leverage the activities and input of SEFA, the UNF Global Alliance for Clean Cookstoves, and their implementing partners. 13. Stronger accountability for actions is required in partnerships like these. The GAVI Alliance’s support for health system strengthening and new vaccine introduction can be utilized at the country level to ensure health worker training, monitoring and evaluation, and supply chain management. 14. Over the past three years, the GAVI Alliance has assisted more than 20 countries in introducing pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV), which prevents the most common cause of childhood pneumonia. 15. Research is essential for effective pneumonia and diarrhoea control efforts. The neglect of research in these fields over the past decade has left many critical clinical and epidemiological questions unanswered. The GAPPD is committed to promoting research, including community-based action research and sociocultural studies on knowledge, attitudes, perceptions, cultural practices, and health-seeking behaviors. 16. As country programs scale up interventions, research will be needed on delivery strategies, overcoming barriers to interventions, and improving implementation methods. However, the need for research should not delay the implementation of effective interventions. 17. Research efforts must also focus on building research capacity in the countries most affected by pneumonia and diarrhoea. 18. The MDGs have generated significant momentum and strengthened political commitment to child survival and development. The reduction in under-five mortality since 1990 has saved millions of young lives, largely through basic health interventions, economic improvement, increased female education, and improved technology. 19. However, much work remains to be done through at least 2025. The GAPPD provides a framework to accelerate progress in preventing and controlling the leading causes of child mortality during the countdown to 2015 and beyond. 20. The opportunity to advocate for and increase investment in pneumonia and diarrhoea should not be missed. Considering the global burden of childhood pneumonia and diarrhoea, the resources required to implement proven interventions are relatively modest. 21. Successful reduction of global health problems requires active involvement of affected communities, supported by effective international partnerships and collaborative efforts. Policies and actions are laying the groundwork for this community-based approach. 22. The global MDG 4 target of reducing child mortality by two-thirds remains out of reach for many of the world’s poorest countries. Approximately 5 billion people lack access to improved sanitation. 23. Targets for improving child health beyond 2015 will not be achieved without urgent action on pneumonia and diarrhoea from national governments and supporting partners at the global level. 24. Focused, coordinated, and integrated international, national, and sub-national action on pneumonia and diarrhoea control, as outlined in the GAPPD, is urgently needed. 25. In a changing world, programs for diarrhoea and pneumonia must be flexible, capable of understanding risks, and adaptable to contextual changes. 26. This document calls on all concerned groups to demonstrate their commitment, allocate the required resources, and work together to make preventable child deaths from pneumonia and diarrhoea a tragedy of the past.
